## Introduction

The primary objective of a Phase I oncology trial is to identify the **maximum tolerated dose (MTD)**, the highest dose whose probability of a **dose-limiting toxicity (DLT)** is judged acceptable. Rule-based designs such as the 3+3 apply fixed escalation and de-escalation rules to the number of DLTs observed in the current cohort. They are simple and transparent, but they do not target an explicit DLT probability and do not borrow information across dose levels through a fitted model. Model-based designs instead fit a dose–toxicity curve to all accumulated data and use that curve to assign each cohort to a dose. The **Bayesian logistic regression model (BLRM)** is a widely used two-parameter model-based approach that is commonly combined with **escalation with overdose control (EWOC)**.

This post describes the BLRM dose-finding design in the [BLRM_trial](https://github.com/cyang728/BLRM_trial) repository. I state the model, the decision rule, and the stopping rules precisely, and then work through one cohort by hand.

## The dose-toxicity model

Let $p_j$ be the DLT probability at dose level $j = 1, \dots, J$, let $d_j$ be the dose, and let $d^\ast$ be a fixed reference dose. BLRM assumes a two-parameter logistic dose–toxicity curve:

$$
\operatorname{logit}(p_j) = \log \alpha + \beta \, \log\!\left(\frac{d_j}{d^\ast}\right).
$$

Phase I dose-finding models conventionally assume that the DLT probability does not decrease with dose. BLRM encodes this as a modeling assumption by requiring the slope $\beta$ to be positive, which makes the dose–toxicity curve strictly increasing. Positivity is imposed on the log scale: the prior is placed on $(\log \alpha, \log \beta)$, so that $\beta = \exp(\log \beta) > 0$ for every value of $\log \beta$.

$$
\theta = (\log \alpha, \, \log \beta)^\top \sim \mathcal{N}_2(\mu, \Sigma).
$$

The prior covariance is

$$
\Sigma =
\begin{pmatrix}
\sigma_1^2 & \rho\,\sigma_1 \sigma_2 \\
\rho\,\sigma_1 \sigma_2 & \sigma_2^2
\end{pmatrix},
$$

where $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ are the prior standard deviations of $\log \alpha$ and $\log \beta$. The repository default is $\mu = (\log 0.5, \, 0) = (-0.693, \, 0)$, $\sigma_1 = 2$, $\sigma_2 = 1$, and $\rho = 0$.

## Toxicity intervals

Partition the unit interval $[0, 1]$ at two cutpoints $0 < c_1 < c_2 < 1$ into three non-overlapping intervals for the DLT probability:

1. an **underdosing interval** $[0, c_1)$,
2. a **target interval** $[c_1, c_2)$,
3. an **overdosing interval** $[c_2, 1]$.

A dose whose DLT probability falls in the target interval is regarded as acceptably dosed, and the MTD is sought there. The repository uses $c_1 = 0.16$ and $c_2 = 0.33$, so the target interval for the MTD is $[0.16, 0.33)$, a common range in Phase I oncology. Given the accumulated data, each dose carries three posterior interval probabilities:

$$
\pi_j^{U} = \Pr(p_j < c_1 \mid \text{data}), \quad
\pi_j^{T} = \Pr(c_1 \le p_j < c_2 \mid \text{data}), \quad
\pi_j^{O} = \Pr(p_j \ge c_2 \mid \text{data}),
$$

and they sum to one, $\pi_j^{U} + \pi_j^{T} + \pi_j^{O} = 1$. Each probability is a posterior probability under the fitted model: the repository draws MCMC samples of $(\log \alpha, \log \beta)$, maps each draw to the DLT probability $p_j$ at every dose, and estimates $\pi_j^{U}$, $\pi_j^{T}$, $\pi_j^{O}$ by the fraction of draws whose $p_j$ falls in the corresponding interval. The whole design is driven by these three numbers at each dose.

## The dose-selection rule

The rule has two ingredients: a safety constraint and a target criterion.

**1. Escalation with overdose control (EWOC).** A dose is *admissible* only if its posterior overdosing probability is below a pre-specified feasibility bound $\eta$:

$$
\mathcal{A} = \{\, j : \pi_j^{O} < \eta \,\}.
$$

A common choice, and the value used by Neuenschwander, Branson, and Gsponer (2008), is $\eta = 0.25$.

**2. Target criterion.** Among the admissible doses, select the one that maximizes the target probability:

$$
j^\ast = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{j \, \in \, \mathcal{A}} \; \pi_j^{T}.
$$

If the current dose level is $j_{\text{cur}}$, the design escalates by at most one level toward $j^\ast$ (to $j_{\text{cur}} + 1$ when $j^\ast > j_{\text{cur}}$), stays when $j^\ast = j_{\text{cur}}$, and de-escalates directly to $j^\ast$ when $j^\ast < j_{\text{cur}}$. The one-level cap applies to escalation only, so the design never skips an untested higher dose, while a dose that is too toxic can be dropped in a single step to the best admissible dose.

::: {.callout-important}
## EWOC constrains dose selection, not only escalation
The admissible set $\mathcal{A}$ is formed first, from the posterior overdosing probability, and $j^\ast$ is chosen inside it. This is the overdose criterion of Neuenschwander, Branson, and Gsponer (2008): the target dose is selected within $\mathcal{A}$, so a dose that violates EWOC is never selected, whether the move would be up, down, or a stay. When the current dose becomes inadmissible, $j^\ast$ lies below it and the design de-escalates to the best admissible dose.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## No dose skipping on escalation
The design escalates by at most one level per cohort, so even when a distant dose maximizes $\pi^{T}$ the next cohort moves only one level up. This prevents skipping over an untested higher dose. The cap does not apply to de-escalation: when safety requires it, the design drops directly to the best admissible dose.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## $j^\ast$ changes every cohort; it is not the MTD
$j^\ast$ is an interim quantity, recomputed after every cohort to choose the next dose. It can move up or down as data accumulate, and one trial passes through many values of $j^\ast$. The **MTD** is different: the single dose declared when the trial stops through the MTD rule below. A trial visits many working targets $j^\ast$ but declares at most one MTD.
:::

## Stopping rules

The trial stops when any one of the following holds.

1. **Declare the MTD.** The current dose $j$ has accumulated enough patients and looks like the target: $\pi_j^{T} \ge p^\ast$ (a target-probability threshold, repository default $p^\ast = 0.5$), the dose is admissible ($\pi_j^{O} < \eta$), $\pi_j^{T}$ is the largest target probability among the treated doses, and the number of patients at $j$ is at least $n_{\min}$ (default 9). The MTD is this dose.
2. **Reach the maximum sample size.** The total sample size reaches $N_{\max}$ without an MTD declaration.
3. **Excessive toxicity.** Every dose is inadmissible, $\pi_j^{O} \ge \eta$ for all $j$, so even the lowest dose is too toxic. The trial stops with no MTD.

::: {.callout-warning}
## A rule that is sometimes quoted but not used here
Some descriptions of BLRM add a rule-based cap, for example stopping if the number of DLTs at any single level exceeds a fixed count. That is **not** part of this implementation, which relies on the three posterior-based rules above. Safety is instead governed by EWOC and by the too-toxic stopping rule, both based on the posterior overdosing probability rather than on a raw DLT count.
:::

## The algorithm in full

Putting the pieces together, the trial runs one cohort at a time. Escalation, staying, and de-escalation are step 6 below; stopping is step 5.

**Initialize.** Set the current dose to the lowest level.

**Then repeat, once per cohort:**

1. Enroll $m$ patients at the current dose and record the number of DLTs.
2. Refit the posterior of $(\log \alpha, \log \beta)$ using **all** data accumulated so far, not just the current cohort.
3. At every dose $j$, compute the three interval probabilities $\pi_j^{U}$, $\pi_j^{T}$, $\pi_j^{O}$.
4. Form the admissible set $\mathcal{A} = \{\, j : \pi_j^{O} < \eta \,\}$ (EWOC).
5. Check the stopping rules, in this order:

    a. **Too toxic.** If $\mathcal{A}$ is empty (every dose has $\pi_j^{O} \ge \eta$), stop with **no MTD**.
    b. **Declare the MTD.** Otherwise, if the current dose is admissible, its $\pi^{T} \ge p^\ast$, its $\pi^{T}$ is the largest among the doses treated so far, and at least $n_{\min}$ patients have been treated at it, stop and declare the current dose the **MTD**.
    c. **Maximum sample size reached.** Otherwise, if the total enrolled has reached $N_{\max}$, stop with **no MTD** (inconclusive).

6. If nothing stopped, set the working target $j^\ast = \arg\max_{j \in \mathcal{A}} \pi_j^{T}$. If $j^\ast$ is above the current dose, escalate by one level (no skipping). If $j^\ast$ equals the current dose, stay. If $j^\ast$ is below the current dose, de-escalate directly to $j^\ast$, the best admissible dose. Then begin the next cohort.

In one sentence: it stops as soon as one of the three checks in step 5 fires; otherwise it updates the current dose as in step 6, escalating by at most one level, staying, or de-escalating directly to the best admissible dose.

## A worked example

Take the repository doses $(10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800)$, reference $d^\ast = 100$, cutpoints $(c_1, c_2) = (0.16, 0.33)$, and the prior above. We use the EWOC feasibility bound $\eta = 0.25$ of Neuenschwander, Branson, and Gsponer (2008). Treat the first cohort of 3 patients at the lowest dose, and suppose we observe **0 DLTs out of 3**.

Given these data, the posterior interval probabilities at each dose are:

|           | Interval    | 10    | 25    | 50    | 100   | 200   | 400   | 800   |
|:----------|:------------|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|
| $\pi^{U}$ | underdosing | 0.913 | 0.811 | 0.658 | 0.409 | 0.236 | 0.157 | 0.113 |
| $\pi^{T}$ | target      | 0.065 | 0.121 | 0.178 | 0.214 | 0.162 | 0.122 | 0.095 |
| $\pi^{O}$ | overdosing  | 0.022 | 0.068 | 0.165 | 0.376 | 0.602 | 0.720 | 0.792 |

Now apply the rule.

- **EWOC.** The admissible doses are those with $\pi^{O} < 0.25$, namely 10, 25, and 50. Dose 100 has $\pi^{O} = 0.376 \ge 0.25$ and is therefore inadmissible at this interim analysis, along with every dose above it.
- **Target.** The largest target probability occurs among the admissible dose levels $j \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ at $j^\ast = 3$, corresponding to dose $d_{j^\ast} = 50$ with $\pi^{T} = 0.178$.
- **Move.** The current dose level is $j_{\text{cur}} = 1$, corresponding to dose 10. Because $j^\ast = 3 > j_{\text{cur}}$, escalation is indicated. Under the no-skipping restriction, the next cohort is assigned to level 2, corresponding to dose **25**.

This example illustrates two points. First, dose 100 can be deemed inadmissible even though it has not yet been administered, because EWOC is based on the posterior dose–toxicity curve rather than on dose-specific observed counts alone. Second, admissibility is reassessed after every cohort, so a dose that is inadmissible at one interim analysis may become admissible later.

![The interim analysis after the first cohort (0 DLTs of 3 at dose 10). Left: the posterior dose–toxicity curve, with the target interval shaded and a 95% credible band. Right: the three posterior interval probabilities at each dose, the EWOC feasibility bound $\eta = 0.25$, and the admissible dose level that maximizes the target probability ($j^\ast$).](blrm_intervals.png)

## Benefits and drawbacks

**Benefits.** BLRM models all accumulated DLT data jointly across dose levels and can improve dose selection relative to algorithmic designs when the model, prior, and decision rules are appropriately calibrated. Its operating characteristics should be evaluated by simulation for the specific trial under consideration.

**Drawbacks.** The decisions are less transparent than a rule-based design. Because Phase I sample sizes are small, BLRM decisions can be sensitive to prior specification and model misspecification. Estimation of a two-parameter dose–toxicity curve may also be less stable than estimation under a one-parameter working model.

## Summary

At each interim analysis, BLRM computes posterior underdosing, target, and overdosing probabilities for every dose. EWOC defines the admissible set, and the dose with the largest target probability within that set is identified as the working target. The actual dose assigned to the next cohort is then determined by the prespecified escalation restriction. In this implementation, the trial stops upon MTD declaration, upon reaching $N_{\max}$ without satisfying the declaration criterion, or when no dose remains admissible.

## References

Babb, J., Rogatko, A., and Zacks, S. (1998). Cancer phase I clinical trials: efficient dose escalation with overdose control. *Statistics in Medicine*, 17(10), 1103–1120.

Neuenschwander, B., Branson, M., and Gsponer, T. (2008). Critical aspects of the Bayesian approach to phase I cancer trials. *Statistics in Medicine*, 27(13), 2420–2439.
